subject: AI borrowing is showing up in Canadian mortgages
bodyMarkdown:
If your mortgage comes up for renewal in the next two years, the number that sets your payment is being decided in the bond market, and the biggest new borrowers in that market are the companies building AI data centres. Moody's has now put that connection in writing.

## Why AI borrowing lands in your renewal

The Globe and Mail reported on Thursday that Moody's has cut its forecast for Canadian house prices next year and now expects only modest gains, and that rising government **bond yields**, the return investors demand for lending money over long stretches, have pushed five-year fixed mortgage rates into the mid-4 per cent range. Canadian Mortgage Trends reported that Moody's Analytics expects fixed rates to climb again in 2027 even if the Bank of Canada holds its policy rate steady for most of the year, and it puts part of that on AI-related borrowing by governments and companies. Goldman Sachs counts five AI bond deals worth US$67 billion since October 29 and US$296 billion of debt issued this year by the companies building the biggest data centres. CNBC reported on November 6 that CoreWeave's bond yield passed 16 per cent. Nvidia racks in Texas and a townhouse in Vaughan are drawing on the same pool of savings.

## What CMHC found in Ontario

The fall mortgage industry report from CMHC, the federal housing agency, says arrears are rising in Ontario, British Columbia and Atlantic Canada and will keep rising through the middle of 2027, with Ontario posting the largest increase and Toronto the most exposed city in the country. CMHC's own summary is that mortgage stress remains contained while regional pressures grow, which I read as a polite way of saying the national average is hiding Ontario. The **mortgage delinquency rate**, the share of mortgages at least 90 days behind on payments, is still low next to past peaks. The pain is concentrated in people renewing contracts they signed when money was nearly free. Moody's has national prices ending the third quarter down 1.1 per cent from a year earlier, with resales off 2.3 per cent from August to September. Falling prices and rising payments at once is the combination nobody plans for.

## The Bank of Canada is leaning the other way

The Bank raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.5 per cent on October 28, its first increase since 2023, to stop high energy prices from spreading into everything else. The summary of deliberations released November 10 says the council thinks it might need to raise rates further and is proceeding carefully, as BNN Bloomberg reported. Variable borrowers paying from about 3.7 per cent, against a prime rate of 4.70 per cent, are therefore watching a central bank that is still tilted upward, with the next decision on December 9. Statistics Canada, meanwhile, says the economy shed 4,700 jobs in October and unemployment reached 6.7 per cent. A central bank that hikes into job losses has decided inflation is the worse of its two problems. For a renewal, though, the five-year bond matters more than the December meeting, and nobody discusses the five-year bond at dinner.

## The takeaway

Statistics Canada publishes October inflation on Monday, and that figure does more than anything else to settle whether December 9 brings a hike or a hold. If you renew before the end of 2027, get a rate hold from your lender in writing this month, because the hold costs nothing and Moody's case is that fixed rates drift up even with the Bank sitting still. Compare the variable rate you can actually get against the fixed rate on offer, since the spread between them is the whole wager. I am watching data centre credit, because if those yields keep climbing, Canadian fixed rates follow whether or not the Bank of Canada ever cuts again.
